# EC2 Auto Scaling: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q009 -->
### Question 1

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The security team has built a new, patched AMI. Every running instance must be replaced with an instance from the new AMI, and at least 90% of the desired capacity must stay in service during the change. The company follows an immutable infrastructure model and does not patch instances in place. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and wait for the group to update the running instances.
- Edit the launch configuration of the group so that it names the new AMI, and let the group apply the edit to the running instances.
- Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and start an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90%.
- Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and terminate the old instances by hand, a few at a time.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and start an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90%.

**Deciding phrases.** "Every running instance must be replaced", "at least 90% of the desired capacity", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: every running instance moves to the new AMI, at least 90% of the capacity stays in service, and nothing is patched in place, because the model is immutable.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a new launch template version plus an instance refresh, because a new version alone changes only the instances that launch later.
4. I remove the edit of the launch configuration, because a launch configuration cannot be modified after it is created. I remove the option that only waits, because the running instances keep their old AMI.
5. Between the instance refresh and terminating the old instances by hand the difference is who does the work; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so the managed refresh wins, and its minimum healthy percentage keeps 90% in service.
6. Check: the instance refresh replaces every instance, keeps 90% of the capacity in service and changes nothing in place. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** An instance refresh is the managed way to replace running instances, for example when [deploying a new Amazon Machine Image (AMI)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-use-cases). Its minimum healthy percentage is the share of [the desired capacity to keep in service](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-min-max-healthy), so a value of 90% matches the stem. Each instance is replaced, not patched, which keeps the model immutable.

**Why not.**

- "Create a launch template version with the new ...": A new version changes later launches only: running instances stay, and new or replacement instances use the [current settings of the Auto Scaling group](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-replacement-uses-current-settings).
- "Edit the launch configuration of the group so ...": You [can't modify a launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-immutable) after you create it, so the edit in this option is not possible.
- "Create a launch template version with the new ...": It works, but someone terminates and watches each batch by hand, while an instance refresh does the same work as one managed operation.

**Twin.** If the stem said "all instances can be replaced at the same time" instead: an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of [0 percent](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-all-at-once).

**Takeaway.** A new launch template version changes future launches; an instance refresh replaces the instances that already run.

**Review.** [An instance refresh replaces running instances to roll out a new version](2-deep.md#an-instance-refresh-replaces-running-instances-to-roll-out-a-new-version-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Traffic follows a predictable daily pattern with a peak every morning; after the peak, the load falls to a level that changes from day to day. The group has one predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode and no other scaling policy. The instances are ready before each morning peak, but the group keeps its peak capacity for the rest of the day and through the night, and the monthly cost has grown. The application must stay ready for the morning peak. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Switch the predictive scaling policy to forecast only mode, so that the policy removes the extra instances when the forecast falls.
- Add a scheduled action each evening that sets the desired capacity to the night level, and keep the predictive scaling policy.
- Add a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and keep the predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode.
- Let predictive scaling raise and lower the maximum capacity of the group automatically when the forecast changes.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and keep the predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode.

**Deciding phrases.** "one predictive scaling policy", "keeps its peak capacity for the rest of the day", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that is MOST cost-effective.
2. I mark the constraints: one predictive policy in forecast and scale mode, the mornings must stay ready, and capacity stays at the peak level for the rest of the day and through the night.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict forecast only mode, because I think that mode lets the forecast remove the extra instances at night.
4. I remove the option that raises and lowers the maximum automatically, because a maximum that predictive scaling raised does not go back down automatically.
5. Between forecast only mode and a target tracking policy the difference is what scales in. My first idea breaks because forecast only mode does not scale the group at all, in either direction, and predictive scaling does not scale in. So the group needs a dynamic policy, and target tracking follows the load, which costs less than a fixed evening action.
6. Check: target tracking plus the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready and removes capacity at night. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Predictive scaling adds instances ahead of the forecast, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in). You can [combine predictive scaling and dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-combine-policy-types-predictive-plus-dynamic): the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready, and the target tracking policy removes instances when the load falls.

**Why not.**

- "Switch the predictive scaling policy to forecast only ...": In [forecast only](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-forecast-only-mode-first) mode the policy forecasts capacity but does not scale the group, so it removes nothing and also stops the morning scale-out.
- "Add a scheduled action each evening that sets ...": It works, but capacity stays at the peak level until the evening, and a fixed night level stays the same while the load changes each day.
- "Let predictive scaling raise and lower the maximum ...": A maximum that predictive scaling raised [does not automatically decrease back](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-raised-max-stays) to the original value, so this setting cannot lower it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "traffic has no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking without the predictive policy, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).

**Takeaway.** Pair predictive scaling with target tracking: predictive scaling adds capacity early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in).

**Review.** [Scheduled and predictive scaling add capacity before the load arrives](2-deep.md#scheduled-and-predictive-scaling-add-capacity-before-the-load-arrives-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs a stateless web application on one Amazon EC2 instance. During the day the load changes often, and at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%. Users then see slow responses. The company expects the number of users to grow during the next year. The application must handle the growth and the daily peaks with minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements?

- Change the instance to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and more memory, and move to a larger type again each time the load grows.
- Turn on detailed monitoring for the instance, so that Amazon CloudWatch publishes the CPU utilization metric every minute instead of every five minutes.
- Run the application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, with a target tracking scaling policy on CPU utilization.
- Attach a second elastic network interface to the instance, so that the instance can accept twice as many user requests during the peaks.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run the application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, with a target tracking scaling policy on CPU utilization.

**Deciding phrases.** "stateless web application on one Amazon EC2 instance", "the load changes often", "minimal downtime"

**Why.** The load changes during the day and grows over time. Horizontal scaling is [essential for dynamic workloads with fluctuating demands](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-decision-guide-horizontal-for-fluctuating), and stateless servers can be [replaced at will without causing an availability impact](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-stateless-servers-replaceable). A group behind a load balancer adds and removes instances while the others keep serving.

**Why not.**

- "Change the instance to a larger instance type ...": To change the type, [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required), so each resize brings downtime, and one instance still serves all users from one place.
- "Turn on detailed monitoring for the instance, so ...": Detailed monitoring reports the metric more often, but it adds no instance, so the single instance still runs out of CPU at the peaks.
- "Attach a second elastic network interface to the ...": A second network interface adds a network path, not vCPUs, so the CPU utilization of the single instance still reaches 100% at the peaks.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the application keeps its state in memory and cannot run as several copies" instead: a larger instance type with a planned stop, because [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) to resize it.

**Takeaway.** For changing load on a stateless tier, scale out with an Auto Scaling group instead of scaling up.

**Review.** [Stopped instances belong in a warm pool not in the running group](2-deep.md#stopped-instances-belong-in-a-warm-pool-not-in-the-running-group-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the results of the target group health checks.
- Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.
- Run a script on each instance that tests the application every minute and calls the Auto Scaling API to mark the instance unhealthy when a test fails.
- Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group waits longer before it checks the health of each new instance.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.

**Deciding phrases.** "uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks", "fails its EC2 system status check", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The hardware fails, so the instance fails its EC2 system status check. EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default) of the group, and the group [automatically terminates it and replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-replaces-impaired-instance). The current settings meet the requirement with no change and no work.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for ...": It works, but it is a change that this failure does not need, because the EC2 status checks of the group already catch impaired hardware.
- "Run a script on each instance that tests ...": It adds code to maintain, and a script on failed hardware stops with the hardware; the default EC2 checks already find this failure.
- "Increase the health check grace period of the ...": The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new instance for failed health; it changes no check.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the target group marks the instance unhealthy, and the instance still passes its EC2 status checks" instead: turn on ELB health checks, because the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) checks by default.

**Takeaway.** Impaired hardware fails the EC2 status checks, and the group acts on those checks with its default settings.

**Review.** [The group replaces instances that fail the health checks you turned on](2-deep.md#the-group-replaces-instances-that-fail-the-health-checks-you-turned-on-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is enabled in Availability Zone A and Availability Zone B. The Auto Scaling group has one subnet, in Availability Zone A, so every instance runs in that zone. The company needs the web tier to be highly available across multiple Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Add a subnet in Availability Zone B to the Auto Scaling group, so that the group places its instances in both zones.
- Add a subnet in Availability Zone C to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the load balancer enabled in zones A and B.
- Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second AWS Region, and register the new instances with the same load balancer.
- Create a second Auto Scaling group with a subnet in Availability Zone B, and attach it to the same target group.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a subnet in Availability Zone B to the Auto Scaling group, so that the group places its instances in both zones.

**Deciding phrases.** "enabled in Availability Zone A and Availability Zone B", "has one subnet, in Availability Zone A", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Instances in one zone share that zone's fate: if it fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances). AWS recommends a group [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-resilience-practices) with the load balancer in the same zones. Zone B is already enabled on the load balancer, so one more subnet in the group completes the design.

**Why not.**

- "Add a subnet in Availability Zone C to ...": The load balancer is not enabled in zone C, and for registered targets in such a zone it [does not route traffic to them](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lb-no-traffic-to-disabled-az).
- "Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second ...": Auto Scaling groups are Regional: they [can span Availability Zones, but not AWS regions](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions).
- "Create a second Auto Scaling group with a ...": It works, but two groups mean two sets of scaling policies and settings to keep in step, and one group can use both zones.

**Twin.** If the stem said "keep running if the whole Region fails" instead: a second group in another Region, because groups are [regional constructs](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions).

**Takeaway.** For high availability, give one Auto Scaling group subnets in several zones that the load balancer also uses.

**Review.** [The group spreads instances evenly across its Availability Zones](2-deep.md#the-group-spreads-instances-evenly-across-its-availability-zones-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. When the group launches an instance, a user data script downloads configuration files for several minutes. The load balancer sends requests to new instances before the script finishes, and users see errors. The company must ensure that no new instance receives traffic before its script ends, and the solution must work automatically for every new instance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group so that it covers the minutes that the user data script needs.
- Turn on slow start for the target group so that each new instance receives a small share of the requests while the script runs.
- Detach the target group from the Auto Scaling group, and use an AWS Lambda function to register each instance after its script reports success.
- Add a launch lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group, and make the user data script call CompleteLifecycleAction after the files are in place.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a launch lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group, and make the user data script call CompleteLifecycleAction after the files are in place.

**Deciding phrases.** "before the script finishes", "no new instance receives traffic before its script ends", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The group [registers your instance with the load balancer](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-registers-with-lb-before-inservice) as the last step before InService. A launch hook holds the new instance in [Pending:Wait](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-hook-states) before that step, so registration waits until the script reports that the application is [ready to accept traffic](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-lb-registration).

**Why not.**

- "Increase the health check grace period of the ...": The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new unhealthy instance; it does not delay registration.
- "Turn on slow start for the target group ...": Slow start still sends requests to the new instance, a smaller share at first, so some users still see errors.
- "Detach the target group from the Auto Scaling ...": It works, but the team writes and runs custom registration code for a pause that a lifecycle hook gives as a group feature.

**Twin.** If the stem said "logs must be copied to Amazon S3 before scale in removes an instance" instead: a termination lifecycle hook, which [pauses the instance before it is terminated](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-scale-in-use).

**Takeaway.** To keep traffic away until setup ends, use a launch lifecycle hook, not the health check grace period.

**Review.** [A new instance joins the load balancer before it becomes InService](2-deep.md#a-new-instance-joins-the-load-balancer-before-it-becomes-inservice-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. A new instance needs several minutes to start before it can serve requests. Traffic follows a predictable pattern: it rises to a peak from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday. Users must not see slow responses during a rise in traffic that can be anticipated. A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable during a rise that cannot be anticipated. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.
- Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.
- Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode that adds and removes instances from its forecast, with no other scaling policy.
- Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of the group to the number of instances that the highest daily peak needs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.

**Deciding phrases.** "from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday", "needs several minutes to start", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The peak is known, and a new instance needs minutes to start, so the capacity is needed before 09:00. Scheduled scaling fits when [the need arises on a predictable schedule](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use). A scheduled action sets [desired, minimum, and maximum capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-action-sets-capacities) at a set time, and target tracking then follows the load inside those limits.

**Why not.**

- "Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps ...": Target tracking is dynamic scaling, [which is reactive in nature](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-long-initialization-fit): the instances start minutes after the 09:00 rise, and users see slow responses.
- "Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and ...": Predictive scaling launches early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in), so a policy that removes instances from its forecast does not exist.
- "Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of ...": It works, but the group pays for the peak capacity outside 09:00 to 11:00 as well, which costs more than scheduled actions.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Traffic rises to a peak several times a day at unpredictable times, with no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking alone, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).

**Takeaway.** A known peak and slow-starting instances: raise capacity with a scheduled action, and let target tracking follow the rest.

**Review.** [Scheduled and predictive scaling add capacity before the load arrives](2-deep.md#scheduled-and-predictive-scaling-add-capacity-before-the-load-arrives-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company uses an Amazon SQS queue to decouple its web tier from an image-processing tier. Worker instances in an Auto Scaling group poll the queue. One worker needs about 2 seconds to process one message, and each message must be processed within 60 seconds after it arrives. The number of uploaded images changes a lot during the day, so the processing tier must be scalable. Which scaling configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- A target tracking scaling policy on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric of the queue, with a target value of 30 messages
- A target tracking scaling policy on the average CPU utilization of the worker group, with a target value of 50 percent
- A fixed group size that matches the number of workers needed at the highest daily upload rate, with no scaling policy
- A target tracking scaling policy on metric math that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with a target value of 30

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** A target tracking scaling policy on metric math that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with a target value of 30

**Deciding phrases.** "about 2 seconds to process one message", "within 60 seconds", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** One worker clears a message in 2 seconds, and a message can wait 60 seconds, so one worker can hold a backlog of 30. AWS says to take the acceptable latency and [divide it by the average time](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target) per message. The metric is the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance): [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math) divided by GroupInServiceInstances, which metric math calculates.

**Why not.**

- "A target tracking scaling policy on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible ...": The queue length [might not change proportionally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the size of the group, so the policy adds the wrong number of workers.
- "A target tracking scaling policy on the average ...": For queue work, AWS says [100% CPU utilization is expected and should not be your primary metric](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-queue-depth-metric-for-batch-work); the queue shows the waiting work.
- "A fixed group size that matches the number ...": It works, but the group pays for peak workers all day; when uploads change, AWS says [you might consider using dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-dynamic-scaling-when-load-varies).

**Twin.** If the stem said "about 6 seconds to process one message" instead: the same metric with a target of 10, because you take the latency and [divide it by the average time](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target).

**Takeaway.** Scale queue workers on backlog per instance; the target is the acceptable latency divided by the time per message.

**Review.** [A worker group scales on the backlog of messages per instance](2-deep.md#a-worker-group-scales-on-the-backlog-of-messages-per-instance-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. A new instance needs several minutes to start before it can serve requests. Traffic rises to a peak several times a day at unpredictable times, with no daily or weekly pattern. Users must not see slow responses during a rise in traffic that can be anticipated. A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable during a rise that cannot be anticipated. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.
- Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.
- Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode that adds and removes instances from its forecast, with no other scaling policy.
- Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of the group to the number of instances that the highest daily peak needs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.

**Deciding phrases.** "at unpredictable times", "A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The peaks have no pattern, so no setting can add instances before them, and the stem accepts a few minutes of slow responses. Target tracking [adjusts the number of EC2 instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-target-tracking-definition) to hold a target, so it follows each peak up and down. Dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).

**Why not.**

- "Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity ...": It works, but the raised weekday minimum pays for extra instances that the stem gives no reason for, because the peaks follow no schedule.
- "Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and ...": [Predictive scaling uses patterns to scale out](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-predictive-patterns-vs-scheduled-times), and [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in), so it fits neither this traffic nor the claim in the option.
- "Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of ...": It works, but the group runs the peak number of instances all day, although the stem accepts a few minutes of slow responses.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Traffic follows a predictable pattern: it rises to a peak from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday" instead: scheduled actions plus target tracking, because you can [use scheduled scaling and scaling policies together](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-plus-policies-together).

**Takeaway.** Peaks at unknown times: use target tracking, which reacts to the load and scales in after it.

**Review.** [Scheduled and predictive scaling add capacity before the load arrives](2-deep.md#scheduled-and-predictive-scaling-add-capacity-before-the-load-arrives-5-min)

</details>

### Question 10

A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the web server process on an instance stops after a memory error, the target group marks the instance unhealthy, and the instance still passes its EC2 status checks. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Leave the health check type of the Auto Scaling group as it is, and rely on the group to replace each instance that it finds unhealthy.
- Install an agent on each instance that tests the web server every minute and reports each failed test to the Auto Scaling API as an unhealthy instance.
- Configure the Application Load Balancer to replace each target that fails its health checks with a new instance from the launch template of the group.
- Set the health check type of the Auto Scaling group to include Elastic Load Balancing, so that the group acts on the health that the target group reports.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Set the health check type of the Auto Scaling group to include Elastic Load Balancing, so that the group acts on the health that the target group reports.

**Deciding phrases.** "uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks", "the target group marks the instance unhealthy, and the instance still passes its EC2 status checks", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The web server stops while the instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks the instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced) and replaces it.

**Why not.**

- "Leave the health check type of the Auto ...": By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, and the instance passes its EC2 status checks, so it stays in service.
- "Install an agent on each instance that tests ...": It works, because a custom check can [mark that particular instance as](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-custom-health-check-immediate-replace) unhealthy, but the team builds and runs an agent that one setting replaces.
- "Configure the Application Load Balancer to replace each ...": A failed check makes the load balancer [stop routing requests to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-elb-requests-before-detection-fail); launching a replacement is work for the group.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check" instead: keep the current settings, because EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default).

**Takeaway.** A running instance whose web server failed needs the ELB health check type on the group.

**Review.** [The group replaces instances that fail the health checks you turned on](2-deep.md#the-group-replaces-instances-that-fail-the-health-checks-you-turned-on-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q008 -->
### Question 11

A company runs long-running video jobs on On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group. Each worker instance takes one job from an Amazon SQS queue, and a job can run for up to 2 hours. The number of jobs changes during the day, and the group scales in when the queue is short. Scale in must not stop a running job. Operators sometimes terminate worker instances by mistake in the Amazon EC2 console, and the company must ensure that this cannot happen. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)

- Turn on instance scale-in protection for every worker instance at all times, so that neither scale in nor the EC2 console can terminate a worker.
- Have each worker turn on instance scale-in protection for its own instance when a job starts, and turn the protection off when the job ends.
- Suspend the Terminate process of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group does not terminate any worker instance when it scales in.
- Turn on Amazon EC2 termination protection for each worker instance that the group launches, so that a termination request from the EC2 console fails.
- Move the workers to Spot Instances, and add a termination lifecycle hook that keeps each Spot Instance running until its current job ends.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Have each worker turn on instance scale-in protection for its own instance when a job starts, and turn the protection off when the job ends.
- Turn on Amazon EC2 termination protection for each worker instance that the group launches, so that a termination request from the EC2 console fails.

**Deciding phrases.** "Scale in must not stop a running job", "terminate worker instances by mistake in the Amazon EC2 console", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Scale in and manual termination are two different paths. For scale in, AWS says to [use instance protection to prevent](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-termination-policy-and-instance-protection) the group from choosing specific instances, and a worker that sets it per job keeps idle workers removable. For the console, you [enable Amazon EC2 termination protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual).

- AWS suggests that you [use instance scale-in protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-unprocessed-messages-return) for long-running workers; with the protection off after each job, the group can remove idle workers.
- Scale-in protection does not cover the console. [To protect Auto Scaling instances from manual termination](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual), you [enable Amazon EC2 termination protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual).

**Why not.**

- "Turn on instance scale-in protection for every worker ...": Scale-in protection does not block a manual termination, and kept on all day it blocks every scale in. For manual termination, AWS says to [enable Amazon EC2 termination protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual).
- "Suspend the Terminate process of the Auto Scaling ...": It protects running jobs, but it gives you [complete control over all EC2 instance terminations](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-suspend-terminate-full-control), so idle workers keep running and the company pays for them.
- "Move the workers to Spot Instances, and add ...": A lifecycle hook [does not prevent an instance from terminating](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice) when Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity, so a long job can stop after a [two-minute interruption notice](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the workers run on Spot Instances" instead: plan for interruptions, because Spot interruptions [bypass all Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling protection mechanisms](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection).

**Takeaway.** Scale-in protection guards against scale in; EC2 termination protection guards against manual termination.

**Review.** [Scale in removes the instance that the termination policy picks](2-deep.md#scale-in-removes-the-instance-that-the-termination-policy-picks-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q010 -->
### Question 12

A company runs a batch application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group was created several years ago from a launch configuration, and it uses one instance type. To lower cost, the company now wants the group to run Spot Instances above a base of On-Demand Instances, and to use several instance types. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Edit the existing launch configuration to add a Spot purchase option and the extra instance types, and keep the group attached to it.
- Create a second launch configuration for the Spot Instances, and attach it to the group next to the current launch configuration.
- Keep the group for the On-Demand base, and create a separate Spot Fleet with several instance types that the team scales with its own scripts.
- Create a launch template with the same settings, and update the group to use it with a mixed instances policy that lists the instance types.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a launch template with the same settings, and update the group to use it with a mixed instances policy that lists the instance types.

**Deciding phrases.** "created several years ago from a launch configuration", "Spot Instances above a base of On-Demand Instances", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A launch configuration cannot create a group that [launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-no-mixed-types); for that you [must use a launch template](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-no-mixed-types). With a mixed instances policy, the group's [base capacity be fulfilled with On-Demand instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above) can stay, and Spot Instances fill the capacity above it.

**Why not.**

- "Edit the existing launch configuration to add a ...": You [can't modify a launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-immutable), and a launch configuration cannot create a group that [launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-no-mixed-types).
- "Create a second launch configuration for the Spot ...": A group can [only specify one launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-launch-configuration-one-and-immutable) at a time, so a second one cannot be attached.
- "Keep the group for the On-Demand base, and ...": It works, but the team runs and scales a second fleet with its own scripts, while one group with a launch template does the same job.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the group already uses a launch template" instead: add a mixed instances policy to the group, because multiple purchase options work [only when you use a launch template](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-purchase-options-need-launch-template).

**Takeaway.** Spot and On-Demand Instances, or several instance types, in one group need a launch template.

**Review.** [A launch template tells the group what to launch in numbered versions](2-deep.md#a-launch-template-tells-the-group-what-to-launch-in-numbered-versions-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q012 -->
### Question 13

A company runs an analytics application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. When an instance starts, the application loads a large data set into memory, which takes about 15 minutes. Traffic rises several times a day at times that are hard to predict, and new instances serve users too late. The instance type supports hibernation. The company wants faster scale-out without paying for running instances that wait for traffic. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Hibernate the instances of the Auto Scaling group when traffic is low, and start them again from hibernation when traffic rises.
- Add a warm pool to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the warm pool instances in the Hibernated state until the group needs them.
- Raise the minimum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to the number of instances that the highest traffic of the day needs.
- Change the launch template to a larger instance type, so that each new instance loads the data set faster and serves more users.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a warm pool to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the warm pool instances in the Hibernated state until the group needs them.

**Deciding phrases.** "loads a large data set into memory", "supports hibernation", "without paying for running instances that wait", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** A warm pool keeps a [pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-definition) beside the group. In the Hibernated state, the instances [save the contents of your RAM](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-hibernated-ram), so the data set is in memory when an instance leaves the pool. No warm pool instance runs while it waits.

**Why not.**

- "Hibernate the instances of the Auto Scaling group ...": [You can't hibernate an instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cannot-hibernate-group-instance) in an Auto Scaling group; the group [marks the stopped instance as unhealthy](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cannot-hibernate-group-instance) and can replace it.
- "Raise the minimum capacity of the Auto Scaling ...": It works, but the group then pays for peak capacity all day, because instances are billed [as soon as they are launched](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-billed-from-launch).
- "Change the launch template to a larger instance ...": A larger instance type still loads the data set at each start, and to change the type of a running instance [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the application starts in a few seconds" instead: no warm pool, because a warm pool that the application does not need [can lead to unnecessary costs](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-unnecessary-cost).

**Takeaway.** Slow start at scale-out: a warm pool of Stopped or Hibernated instances, not hibernation inside the group.

**Review.** [Stopped instances belong in a warm pool not in the running group](2-deep.md#stopped-instances-belong-in-a-warm-pool-not-in-the-running-group-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q014 -->
### Question 14

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group has one simple scaling policy that adds two instances when average CPU utilization is above 70%, and the group uses the default cooldown. Traffic is spiky. When a second spike comes a few minutes after the first one, the group adds no instances until the cooldown ends. New instances also show high CPU utilization while they start, which once caused a scale-out that was not needed. Which change will solve both problems in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Keep the simple scaling policy, and lower the default cooldown of the group to 60 seconds, so that the policy can react to each new spike sooner.
- Replace the simple scaling policy with a target tracking scaling policy, and lower the default cooldown, because the new policy also waits for the cooldown.
- Replace the simple scaling policy with a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and turn on a default instance warmup for the group.
- Keep the simple scaling policy, and raise the minimum capacity of the group to the number of instances that the largest spike needs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Replace the simple scaling policy with a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and turn on a default instance warmup for the group.

**Deciding phrases.** "simple scaling policy", "adds no instances until the cooldown ends", "high CPU utilization while they start", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The cooldown applies to [scaling activities initiated by simple scaling policies](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cooldown-applies-to-simple-scaling). Target tracking uses a warmup instead: a new instance is [not counted toward the aggregated EC2 instance metrics](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warmup-instance-not-in-metrics) until its warmup ends. The new policy reacts to the second spike, and start-up load starts no extra scale-out.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the simple scaling policy, and lower the ...": A shorter cooldown lets the start-up load of new instances start even more scale-outs, and AWS advises: [do not use simple scaling policies](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-simple-scaling-not-recommended).
- "Replace the simple scaling policy with a target ...": Target tracking scales out [without waiting for the cooldown period to end](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cooldown-target-tracking-step-do-not-wait), so a lower cooldown changes nothing, and without a warmup the start-up load still counts.
- "Keep the simple scaling policy, and raise the ...": It works for the spikes, but the group then pays for the capacity of the largest spike all day, also when traffic is low.

**Twin.** If the stem said "traffic rises at the same time every weekday" instead: also add a scheduled action before that time, because scheduled scaling fits when [the need arises on a predictable schedule](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).

**Takeaway.** Cooldowns belong to simple scaling; target tracking and step scaling use an instance warmup.

**Review.** [Step scaling follows alarm size and warmup replaces the old cooldown](2-deep.md#step-scaling-follows-alarm-size-and-warmup-replaces-the-old-cooldown-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q016 -->
### Question 15

A company has an Auto Scaling group that runs On-Demand Instances of one instance type in two Availability Zones. The group uses the default termination policy. Availability Zone A has three instances: two were launched from the current version of the launch template, and one from an older version. Availability Zone B has two instances from the current version, and one of them is the oldest instance in the group. No instance has scale-in protection. The group now scales in by one instance. Which instance does the group terminate?

- The instance in Availability Zone A that was launched from the older version of the launch template.
- The instance in Availability Zone B that is the oldest instance in the group, because it has run the longest.
- The newest instance in Availability Zone A, because the group removes the most recent launch first.
- One instance chosen at random from all five instances, because the default termination policy treats every zone the same.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** The instance in Availability Zone A that was launched from the older version of the launch template.

**Deciding phrases.** "default termination policy", "Availability Zone A has three instances", "one of them is the oldest instance in the group"

**Why.** First, the group picks the Availability Zone that [has the most instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-zone-with-most): Zone A, with three. Inside Zone A, the default policy is designed to [terminate instances that are using outdated configurations first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-outdated-first). The instance from the older launch template version is the outdated one.

**Why not.**

- "The instance in Availability Zone B that is ...": The group [always balances instances across Availability Zones first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-az-balance-first), and [OldestInstance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policy-oldest-instance) is a policy that you choose, not the default.
- "The newest instance in Availability Zone A, because ...": To [terminate the newest instance in the group](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policy-newest-instance) is the rule of the NewestInstance policy, which you choose; the default policy looks for outdated configurations.
- "One instance chosen at random from all five ...": The default policy first picks the zone that [has the most instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-zone-with-most), and a random choice comes last, among instances [closest to the next billing hour](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-billing-hour-then-random).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the group uses the OldestInstance termination policy" instead: the oldest instance of Zone A, because the group [always balances instances across Availability Zones first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-az-balance-first).

**Takeaway.** On scale in, zone balance comes first; then the default policy removes outdated configurations.

**Review.** [Scale in removes the instance that the termination policy picks](2-deep.md#scale-in-removes-the-instance-that-the-termination-policy-picks-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q020 -->
### Question 16

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking scaling policy. Traffic follows the same daily pattern, with a peak every afternoon, and new instances need several minutes before they serve users. The group has 3 weeks of metric history. The operations team plans to create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan for the group, only to get predictive scaling. Which solution will add predictive scaling with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan for the application, and turn on predictive scaling for the Auto Scaling group inside the plan.
- Add a predictive scaling policy directly to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the target tracking scaling policy that the group uses today.
- Register the Auto Scaling group as a scalable target in Application Auto Scaling, and attach a predictive scaling policy to that target.
- Write an AWS Lambda function that reads the metric history each day and creates scheduled actions for the expected afternoon peak.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a predictive scaling policy directly to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the target tracking scaling policy that the group uses today.

**Deciding phrases.** "same daily pattern", "only to get predictive scaling", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A predictive scaling policy is a [native scaling policy in EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-policy-vs-scaling-plan), so the team does not have to [create an AWS Auto Scaling plan](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-policy-vs-scaling-plan) for it. The policy can [proactively increase capacity ahead of upcoming demand](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-ahead-of-demand), and the target tracking policy keeps following the load.

**Why not.**

- "Create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan for ...": It works, but AWS recommends predictive policies [directly on your Auto Scaling resources instead](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-plans-prefer-native-predictive-policies) of a plan used only for predictive scaling.
- "Register the Auto Scaling group as a scalable ...": For EC2 instances, [use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-wa-ec2-auto-scaling-for-instances-application-auto-scaling-for-other-services); Application Auto Scaling is for other services, such as Amazon ECS.
- "Write an AWS Lambda function that reads the ...": It can work for a fixed pattern, but the team writes and runs code that a predictive scaling policy replaces with one setting.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the group has 6 hours of metric history" instead: keep target tracking for now, because predictive scaling needs [at least 24 hours of data](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-needs-24-hours-of-data).

**Takeaway.** Predictive scaling for an EC2 group is a policy of the group itself, without a scaling plan.

**Review.** [AWS Auto Scaling](2-services.md#aws-auto-scaling-1-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q022 -->
### Question 17

A company runs image-processing workers on Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group. The jobs can tolerate interruption, because an unfinished job returns to the queue. When Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity, the group loses several workers at once, and the replacements start only after the old instances are gone. The backlog then grows for several minutes. The company wants to keep Spot pricing. Which change will make the worker group MOST resilient to Spot interruptions?

- Add a termination lifecycle hook to the group, so that Amazon EC2 waits until each worker finishes its current job before it reclaims the instance.
- Turn on instance scale-in protection for every worker instance, so that Amazon EC2 does not reclaim a worker while it processes a job.
- Turn on Capacity Rebalancing for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group launches a new Spot Instance when a running one is at risk.
- Change the Spot allocation strategy of the group to lowest-price, so that the group launches its workers from the cheapest Spot pools.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on Capacity Rebalancing for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group launches a new Spot Instance when a running one is at risk.

**Deciding phrases.** "the replacements start only after the old instances are gone", "keep Spot pricing", "MOST resilient"

**Why.** Without Capacity Rebalancing, the group waits [until after the Amazon EC2 Spot service interrupts](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-no-capacity-rebalancing-replace-after-interruption) an instance before it replaces it. With Capacity Rebalancing, the group starts a replacement when an instance is [at an elevated risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-capacity-rebalancing-spot), while the old worker still runs.

**Why not.**

- "Add a termination lifecycle hook to the group, ...": A lifecycle hook [does not prevent an instance from terminating](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice) when Spot capacity is reclaimed; the worker gets a [two-minute interruption notice](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice).
- "Turn on instance scale-in protection for every worker ...": Spot interruptions [bypass all Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling protection mechanisms](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection), scale-in protection included.
- "Change the Spot allocation strategy of the group ...": It keeps Spot pricing, but the lowest-price strategy has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-lowest-price-not-recommended), so more workers stop.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the workers keep state that cannot be lost" instead: On-Demand Instances, because Amazon EC2 [can interrupt and reclaim your instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection) in a Spot group.

**Takeaway.** To replace Spot workers before they are interrupted, turn on Capacity Rebalancing.

**Review.** [A mixed instances group adds Spot capacity on top of an On-Demand base](2-deep.md#a-mixed-instances-group-adds-spot-capacity-on-top-of-an-on-demand-base-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=auto-scaling-q021 -->
### Question 18

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The Region has three Availability Zones. At peak load, the application needs 6 instances. The application must be fault tolerant across multiple Availability Zones: if one zone fails, 6 instances must keep serving requests with no wait for new instances. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)

- Keep the minimum capacity at 6 instances, and rely on the group to launch replacement instances in the other zones after a zone fails.
- Configure the Auto Scaling group and the load balancer to use subnets in three Availability Zones of the Region.
- Configure the group to use two Availability Zones, and set the minimum capacity to 12 instances, with 6 in each zone.
- Set the minimum capacity of the group to 9 instances, so that each of the three Availability Zones runs 3 instances.
- Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second AWS Region, and keep 6 instances in each Region behind the same load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Configure the Auto Scaling group and the load balancer to use subnets in three Availability Zones of the Region.
- Set the minimum capacity of the group to 9 instances, so that each of the three Availability Zones runs 3 instances.

**Deciding phrases.** "fault tolerant", "with no wait for new instances", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Fault tolerant here means no wait after a zone fails, so the spare capacity runs before the failure. Well-Architected says [static stability is preferred for high availability](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-static-stability-for-az-loss) when a whole zone is lost. Three zones with three instances each still leave six after one zone fails, with the fewest instances.

- AWS recommends a group [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-resilience-practices) with the load balancer in the same zones; three zones keep the spare share small.
- Nine instances in three zones leave six when one zone fails, so the peak load is served with no launch and no wait.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the minimum capacity at 6 instances, and ...": Replacements arrive [within minutes](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-replacement-time-minutes), so users wait for capacity; that is high availability, not the fault tolerance that the stem asks for.
- "Configure the group to use two Availability Zones, ...": It works, but two zones need six instances each, twelve in all, which costs more than nine instances across three zones.
- "Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second ...": An Auto Scaling group [can span Availability Zones, but not AWS regions](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions), so one group cannot extend into a second Region.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a short wait for new instances is acceptable" instead: six instances across the zones, because the group can [launch instances in another one to compensate](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-az-unavailable-launch-elsewhere).

**Takeaway.** Fault tolerant across zones: size the group so that the remaining zones carry the peak without new launches.

**Review.** [The group spreads instances evenly across its Availability Zones](2-deep.md#the-group-spreads-instances-evenly-across-its-availability-zones-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
